metadata.title: Considerations in Demonstrating Interchangeability With a Reference Product: Update
metadata.topic: Draft guideline · FDA human drugs and biologics
metadata.legal_basis: FDA Guidance Document (21 CFR 10.115). Guidance states FDA's current thinking and is not binding unless a statute or regulation requires it; the official text governs.

metadata_verification: Source-register metadata; dates and legal status require human verification.

candidates.statement: In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities. 40 Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a topic and should be viewed only 41 as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited. The use of 42 the word should in Agency guidances means that something is suggested or recommended, but 43 not required. 44
candidates.context: This draft guidance is not intended to be finalized as a standalone guidance. Instead, the 34 recommendations in this draft guidance, when finalized, are intended to revise the 35 Interchangeability Guidance and to replace certain sections in that document, such as sections 36 VI.A and VII, to reflect FDA’s current thinking regarding the subject addressed in this guidance. 37 FDA is issuing this draft guidance to seek public comment through the accompanying docket. 38

candidates.statement: A biosimilar product must, among other things, be demonstrated to be highly similar to the 57 reference product, notwithstanding minor differences in clinically inactive components, and have 58 no clinically meaningful differences from the reference product in terms of the safety, purity, and 59 potency of the product. 8 Additionally, the proposed biosimilar product must be shown to have 60 the same mechanism(s) of action as the reference product (but only to the extent known for the 61 reference product), same route of administration, same dosage form, and same strength as the 62 reference product, and may be licensed only for conditions of use that have been previously 63 licensed for the reference product. 9 Typically, the data and information supporting a 64
candidates.context: The Biologics Price Competition and Innovation Act of 2009 (BPCI Act) amended the PHS Act 49 and other statutes to create an abbreviated licensure pathway for biological products shown to be 50 biosimilar to, or interchangeable with, an FDA-licensed biological reference product (see 51 sections 7001 through 7003 of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (Public Law 111– 52 148). Section 351(k) of the PHS Act (42 U.S.C. 262(k)), added by the BPCI Act, sets forth the 53 requirements for the licensure of a proposed biosimilar or proposed interchangeable biosimilar 54 product. 55 5 Herndon, TM, Ausin C, Brahme NN, Schrieber SJ, Luo M, Andrada FC, Kim C, Sun W, Zhou L, Grosser S, Yim S, and Ricci MS, 2023, Safety Outcomes When Switching Between Biosimilars and Reference Biologics: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis, PLoS ONE, 18(10):e0292231. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.02

candidates.statement: The BPCI Act distinguishes between biosimilar products and biosimilar products that are 77 interchangeable with the corresponding reference product with respect to the standards that must 78 be met for approval and the effect of such approvals. For an interchangeable biosimilar, in 79 addition to meeting the requirements for biosimilarity, FDA must determine that the information 80 submitted in the application or supplement is sufficient to show 1) that the biological product can 81 be expected to produce the same clinical result as the reference product in any given patient, 10
candidates.context: determination of biosimilarity includes a rigorous and comprehensive comparison of 65 physicochemical and biological functional attributes of a proposed biosimilar to its reference 66 product, along with one or more clinical studies that includes an assessment of immunogenicity. 67 FDA generally expects that applications for proposed biosimilar biological products will include 68 an assessment of immunogenicity. This assessment may include information to address the 69 possibility that treatment with one biological product (e.g., the proposed biosimilar) following 70 treatment with another biological product (e.g., the reference product) may affect a patient’s 71 immune response to the treatment. Once a biosimilar is licensed, healthcare providers can 72 prescribe the biosimilar product to patients who have not previously received the reference 73 product (i.e., treatment-naïve patients)

candidates.statement: • Applicants may choose to provide an assessment of why the comparative analytical and 109 clinical data provided in the application or supplement support a showing that the 110 switching standard set forth in section 351(k)(4)(B) of the PHS Act has been met. Any 111 such assessment should include any other information the applicant considers relevant to 112 support a showing that the risk, in terms of safety and diminished efficacy, from 113 alternating or switching between the reference product and the proposed interchangeable 114 product is not greater than the risk of using the reference product without such 115 alternation or switch. 116
candidates.context: Therefore, FDA intends to revise the Interchangeability Guidance consistent with the scientific 105 approach discussed above and has the following recommendations to applicants for proposed 106 interchangeable biosimilar products: 107 • Applicants with a pending 351(k) BLA for a proposed biosimilar product may choose to 118 submit an amendment to their pending BLA with the above-described assessment along 119 with any additional data and/or information that they consider relevant to address the 120 requirements in section 351(k)(4) of the PHS Act and request that their BLA be reviewed 121 as a proposed interchangeable biosimilar. 13 , 14
